title: Exploring the Iris Dataset
text:
Exploring the Iris Dataset
This story explores the famous Iris dataset using R and ggplot2.

Source: Wikimedia




Let’s explore the Iris flowers dataset. 




The Iris dataset contains measurements of sepal length, sepal width, petal length, and petal width for 150 iris flowers, along with their species. It’s a classic dataset for classification and data exploration.




Let’s start by visualizing the distribution of sepal length for each species. We can see that setosa generally has shorter sepals than versicolor and virginica.




Next, let’s examine the petal length. Here, the differences between species are even more pronounced, with setosa having much shorter petals.




Now, let’s look at the relationship between sepal length and sepal width, colored by species. We can observe some clustering, particularly for setosa. 




Finally, let’s visualize the relationship between petal length and petal width. This plot clearly shows three distinct clusters, making it easy to separate the species based on these two features. 




This exploration demonstrates how the Iris dataset, despite its simplicity, provides a great foundation for understanding data visualization and basic machine learning concepts.

title: Iris Machine Learning Project
section: Create feature matrix and target vector
text:
Create feature matrix and target vector

X <- iris[, 1:4]
y <- iris$Species

title: Iris Machine Learning Project
text:
Split the data (70% train, 30% test)

set.seed(42)
train_index <- createDataPartition(y, p = 0.7, list = FALSE)
X_train <- X[train_index, ]
X_test  <- X[-train_index, ]
y_train <- y[train_index]
y_test  <- y[-train_index]

title: Iris Machine Learning Project
text:
Standardize features

# Calculate mean and sd manually for each column
scaling_params <- data.frame(
  feature = colnames(X_train),
  mean = apply(X_train, 2, mean),
  sd = apply(X_train, 2, sd)
)

# Display scaling parameters
scaling_params |> 
  gt() |> 
  tab_header(title = "Scaling Parameters") |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(mean, sd), decimals = 4)

# Apply scaling
X_train_scaled <- scale(X_train, center = scaling_params$mean, scale = scaling_params$sd)
X_test_scaled <- scale(X_test, center = scaling_params$mean, scale = scaling_params$sd)

title: Iris Machine Learning Project
text:
Train a Random Forest classifier

set.seed(42)
model <- randomForest(x = X_train_scaled, 
                     y = y_train, 
                     ntree = 100, 
                     importance = TRUE)

title: Iris Machine Learning Project
text:
Make predictions

y_pred <- predict(model, X_test_scaled)

title: Iris Machine Learning Project
text:
Evaluate the model

accuracy <- sum(y_pred == y_test) / length(y_test)
cat("Model Accuracy:", sprintf("%.2f%%", accuracy * 100), "\n")

Model Accuracy: 93.33%

Classification Report

title: Iris Machine Learning Project
text:
Confusion Matrix for Plotting

cm <- table(Actual = y_test, Predicted = y_pred)
cm_df <- as.data.frame(cm)

title: Iris Machine Learning Project
text:
Plot 1: Confusion Matrix

confusion_plot <- ggplot(cm_df, aes(x = Predicted, y = Actual, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = Freq), color = "white", size = 12, fontface = "bold") +
  labs(title = "Confusion Matrix", 
       x = "Predicted Species", 
       y = "Actual Species",
       fill = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()

confusion_plot

title: Iris Machine Learning Project
text:
Feature importance

feature_importance <- data.frame(
  feature = rownames(importance(model)),
  importance = importance(model)[, "MeanDecreaseGini"]
) %>%
  arrange(desc(importance))

feature_importance |> 
  gt() |> 
  tab_header(title = "Feature Importance") |>
  fmt_number(columns = importance, decimals = 4)

Plot 2: Feature Importance

importance_plot <- ggplot(feature_importance, 
                         aes(x = reorder(feature, importance), y = importance)) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.8, fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Feature Importance in Random Forest Model",
       x = "Feature",
       y = "Importance Score") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

importance_plot

title: Iris Machine Learning Project
text:
Create predictions DataFrame for visualization

test_results <- as.data.frame(X_test)
colnames(test_results) <- colnames(X)
test_results$actual <- y_test
test_results$predicted <- y_pred
test_results$correct <- test_results$actual == test_results$predicted

title: Iris Machine Learning Project
section: Plot 3: Prediction Results (using first two features)
text:
Plot 3: Prediction Results (using first two features)

prediction_plot <- ggplot(test_results, 
                         aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Sepal.Width, 
                             color = predicted, shape = actual)) +
  geom_point(size = 4, alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "Model Predictions on Test Set",
       x = "Sepal Length (cm)",
       y = "Sepal Width (cm)",
       color = "Predicted",
       shape = "Actual") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

prediction_plot
